title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 1,428 cleaned smart-meter readings for 2024 shows total consumption of 1,207,700 kWh across 12 meters. Industrial buildings dominate usage, accounting for over 82% of all consumption. Quarterly demand peaked in Q4 and Q1, reflecting seasonal heating patterns. Second-half consumption rose ~4.7% versus the first half. Commercial load on hot days is modest, and a moderate negative temperature–consumption correlation exists for commercial sites. Peak and off-peak tariff splits are nearly equal.

key_findings.statement: Across all 1,428 readings in the cleaned dataset, total electricity consumption reached 1,207,700 kWh, with a mean of 845.7 kWh per reading.

Industrial buildings consumed 995,362 kWh (82.4% of total), far exceeding Commercial at 196,367 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,971 kWh (1.3%). The ranking from highest to lowest is Industrial, Commercial, Residential.

Quarterly consumption shows a U-shaped pattern: Q4 was highest at 352,882 kWh, followed by Q1 (319,678 kWh), Q2 (270,277 kWh), and Q3 (264,863 kWh) — the lowest quarter. The ranking from highest to lowest is Q4, Q1, Q2, Q3.
Second-half consumption (617,745 kWh, July–December) exceeded first-half consumption (589,955 kWh, January–June) by approximately 27,790 kWh, representing an increase of 4.7%.

On hot days (temperature ≥ 25 °C), there were 19 commercial readings with a mean consumption of 415.3 kWh per reading — below the overall dataset mean of 845.7 kWh, suggesting commercial sites do not exhibit elevated load under high-temperature conditions in this dataset.

The distribution of consumption is right-skewed: the median is 406.8 kWh while the standard deviation is 913.4 kWh, indicating a wide spread driven by high-consumption industrial meters. The mean temperature across readings with valid data is 11.6 °C; 62 readings have missing temperature values. For commercial sites, the Pearson correlation between temperature and consumption is −0.64, a moderate negative relationship suggesting lower commercial consumption at higher temperatures.

Off-peak tariff consumption (608,076 kWh) marginally exceeded peak tariff consumption (599,624 kWh), with peak accounting for 49.7% of total usage — an almost even split. The dataset covers 12 distinct meters; the highest-consuming single meter recorded 252,241 kWh, representing 20.9% of total consumption. The tariff ranking from highest to lowest is off-peak, peak.

limitations: 62 readings (4.3% of the dataset) have missing temperature values, which may introduce bias into temperature-based analyses, particularly the commercial temperature–consumption correlation.
Only 19 commercial readings qualify as hot-day observations (temperature ≥ 25 °C), making the hot-day commercial load estimate statistically fragile.
The dataset covers only 12 distinct meters, limiting the generalisability of findings to the broader meter population.
Residential consumption is very low relative to other building types (1.3% of total), which may reflect under-representation of residential meters rather than true consumption patterns.
The analysis uses calendar quarters and half-years; seasonal effects may not align perfectly with these fixed boundaries.
Correlation does not imply causation; the negative commercial temperature–consumption relationship may be confounded by other variables not present in the dataset.
conclusion: Industrial sites drive the vast majority of electricity consumption in 2024, and demand follows a seasonal U-shape with peaks in Q4 and Q1. Second-half consumption grew modestly (+4.7%) relative to the first half. Peak and off-peak tariff usage is nearly balanced. The wide standard deviation and skewed distribution highlight the outsized influence of a small number of high-consumption industrial meters. Improving temperature data completeness and expanding meter coverage would strengthen future analyses.
